MIAMI, Florida (CNN) -- A Florida boy remains in stable condition just days after he found his parents' long-forgotten handgun in a closet and accidentally shot himself in the head. Police are deciding whether or not to charge parents after their son found a forgotten gun and shot himself. Sheriff's detectives in Pinellas County, Florida, near St. Petersburg, say the boy found the .25-caliber European semi-automatic handgun in a box in a closet in their home. "They are dealing with this very tragic situation, and at this point, no charges have been filed," said Cecilia Barreda of the Pinellas County sheriff's office. His stepfather found Jacob Larson, 12, with a gunshot wound to the head Friday. The stepfather called 911. Police say the shooting took place between 7:40 a.m., when his mother, Tracy Newman, leaves for work, and about 11 a.m., when his stepfather, Joseph Newton, returns home. The boy normally goes to school about 8:30 a.m. "A few years ago, they moved, and [the gun] was stored in the closet. The mother never checked it, never fired it," Barreda said. "They told detectives that they forgot they had stored it in a box inside a closet. Both her and her husband forgot about it," she said. Newman told detectives that she received the gun six years ago from a former employer. Police say that both she and her husband are cooperating in the investigation into the incident. The sheriff's office says it's unlikely that they will face charges. Florida law prohibits a person from leaving a loaded firearm where a minor might have access to it. Prosecutors do have some discretion, and depending on what happens with the gun, charges ranging from a misdemeanor to a felony can be filed in the event of death or serious injury. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention say that 17 states have child firearm access protection and safe-storage laws. Chief Assistant State Attorney Bruce Bartlett says that although laws are needed, an accident with a firearm can be a greater penalty than any judge could ever hand down. "Sometimes, the injury of a child is more severe from a punishment standpoint than any kind of criminal charge," he said. The CDC says three children per day, on average, died in accidental incidents in the United States from 2000 to 2005, the last year data are available. Bartlett said his office has filed charges in previous cases when there was culpable negligence on the part of a gun owner. But, he says, there are cases where accidents happen, not crimes. The Brady Campaign to Prevent Gun Violence says that 34 percent of children in the United States live in homes with at least one firearm, so people have to be aware. "It's a horrible thing, and those parents will blame themselves from here out, and you have to look at things real close to see if it warrants any enforcement from our end," Bartlett said.

# When Home Isn't Safe: The Hidden Toll of Unsecured Firearms

*An examination of family gun accidents involving children and the patchwork of laws meant to prevent them*

---

The morning of a firearm accident rarely arrives with warning. In households across America, guns kept for protection, sport, or collection sit in nightstands, closets, and glove compartments—often loaded, frequently unlocked. When a child finds one, the consequences can be irreversible in seconds.

## The Scope of the Problem

Firearm-related injuries have become a leading cause of death for American children and adolescents. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), firearms surpassed motor vehicle crashes as the leading cause of death among people ages 1 to 19 in recent years—a shift that public health experts describe as a national emergency.

While a substantial portion of these deaths involve homicides and suicides, unintentional shootings represent a preventable category that draws particular attention from safety advocates. The CDC's data on unintentional firearm deaths shows that hundreds of Americans die each year in accidental shootings, with children disproportionately represented among the youngest victims. Many of these incidents occur in the home, involving firearms belonging to a parent or relative.

Gun safety organizations have long sought to quantify the risks. The Brady Campaign to Prevent Gun Violence has estimated that millions of American children live in homes with firearms, and that a significant share of those weapons are stored loaded and unlocked. Brady's research and advocacy have emphasized that access, more than the mere presence of a gun, drives the risk of unintentional injury.

## How Accidents Happen

Child-access shootings tend to follow recognizable patterns. A young child, curious and unable to distinguish a real weapon from a toy, discovers a handgun in a drawer or bag. Older children and teenagers, aware of a gun's location, may handle it believing it to be unloaded.

Researchers who study these cases point to two consistent factors: the developmental inability of young children to appreciate danger, and the frequent overestimation by adults of a child's ability to leave a discovered firearm alone. Studies have repeatedly found that children who know where a gun is kept, and who have been instructed not to touch it, will still handle the weapon when they encounter it unsupervised.

The moments surrounding these incidents are often ordinary—a parent in another room, a brief errand, a sleepover at a relative's house. The interval between discovery and tragedy can be a matter of minutes.

## Florida's Legal Framework

Florida occupies a notable place in the history of firearm storage legislation. In 1989, it became one of the first states to enact a Child Access Prevention (CAP) law, following a series of accidental shootings involving children that drew statewide attention.

Under Florida law, a person who stores or leaves a loaded firearm within reach or easy access of a minor may face criminal liability if the minor gains access and uses the weapon to cause injury or death, or displays it in a public place. The statute generally applies when the firearm is kept in a manner that the owner knew or should have known made it accessible to a child.

The law includes exceptions—for instance, when the firearm is stored in a securely locked container, when it is carried on the owner's person, or when a minor obtains the weapon through unlawful entry. Violations can be charged as misdemeanors or, in cases involving serious harm, elevated depending on the circumstances.

Florida law also requires that firearm dealers provide certain warnings about safe storage at the point of sale, reinforcing the state's emphasis on owner responsibility.

Safety advocates credit CAP laws with contributing to reductions in unintentional child shootings in some studies, while critics and enforcement officials note that such laws often come into play only after a tragedy has occurred. The deterrent value, they argue, depends heavily on public awareness and consistent enforcement.

## The Debate Over Prevention

The question of how to reduce family gun accidents sits at the intersection of public health, law, and personal liberty.

Gun safety organizations advocate for a combination of measures: mandatory safe-storage requirements, distribution of gun locks, public education campaigns, and pediatrician counseling on firearm safety. Programs that provide free or subsidized locking devices have expanded in many communities, and some hospitals now incorporate storage discussions into routine child wellness visits.

Firearm owners' groups and many gun owners emphasize education and voluntary responsibility over mandates. They point to programs designed to teach both adults and children about firearm safety, and they raise concerns that storage requirements could impede a homeowner's ability to access a weapon quickly for self-defense. This tension—between rapid accessibility and secure storage—remains a central point of disagreement.

Public health researchers tend to frame the issue in terms of layered prevention: no single measure eliminates risk, but the combination of secure storage, technology such as lockboxes and personalized firearms, and cultural norms around responsible ownership can meaningfully reduce harm.

## A Preventable Category

What distinguishes unintentional child shootings from many other forms of gun violence is the broad consensus that they should not happen. Across the political spectrum, few defend the practice of leaving a loaded firearm where a toddler can reach it.

The CDC and independent researchers continue to study which interventions work best, and organizations like the Brady Campaign continue to press for policy changes and public awareness. Meanwhile, states have adopted a patchwork of approaches, with Florida's early CAP law standing as one model among many.

For families, the practical guidance offered by safety experts is consistent: store firearms unloaded, locked, and separate from ammunition; use a gun safe or lockbox; and treat access—not merely instruction—as the primary line of defense.

The statistics, however grim, describe a problem that experts across disciplines agree is addressable. Behind each number is a household that, in most cases, never imagined tragedy could arrive in the space of an unattended moment.

---

*Readers seeking information on safe firearm storage can consult resources from the CDC, state law enforcement agencies, and gun safety organizations. Free gun locks are available through many local programs and law enforcement offices.*

---

**A note on sourcing:** This article references general findings from the CDC on firearm mortality among children and adolescents and from the Brady Campaign on household firearm access. For a publication-ready piece, specific figures should be verified against the most current CDC WISQARS data and the latest Brady Campaign publications, and the summary of Florida law should be confirmed against the current text of the relevant Florida Statutes and recent case law.

*Editor's note: This is a fictional news story created for illustrative purposes.*

A 4-year-old boy died Tuesday after finding a handgun in a bedroom closet and accidentally shooting himself, authorities said, in a case that has thrown a spotlight on the contentious question of when—and whether—parents should be held criminally responsible for such tragedies.

The child, whose name is being withheld by police, was at home with a family member when he discovered the loaded weapon on a shelf, according to the county sheriff's office. Investigators say the gun had been placed there years earlier and was largely forgotten by the family.

"This is every parent's worst nightmare," Sheriff's spokesperson Maria Delgado said at a news conference. "But part of our job is to determine whether this was a preventable tragedy and whether the law requires accountability."

## A Question of Charges

The district attorney's office confirmed it is reviewing the circumstances to decide whether charges are warranted—a decision that legal experts say is far from straightforward.

At least 26 states have some form of child access prevention law, which can hold adults liable when a minor gains access to an improperly secured firearm. Penalties range from misdemeanors to felonies, depending on the outcome.

"The trend over the past decade has been toward greater accountability," said Jonathan Reyes, a professor of criminal law who studies firearm legislation. "Prosecutors are increasingly willing to bring charges, particularly when a death results. The reasoning is that safe storage is a legal duty, not just a moral one."

## Grief Versus Punishment

Others argue that prosecuting grieving parents compounds one tragedy with another.

"There is no punishment a court could impose that exceeds what these parents are already living with," said Karen Whitfield, a family advocate who counsels survivors of accidental shootings. "Losing a child is a life sentence. We should be asking how to prevent the next one, not how to punish the last."

Whitfield and others contend that criminal charges may discourage families from cooperating with investigators and could disproportionately affect households already facing hardship.

## Prevention Advocates Weigh In

Gun safety organizations point to the incident as evidence of a broader problem. An estimated 4.6 million American children live in homes with at least one loaded, unlocked firearm, according to research cited by safety groups.

"Safe storage saves lives—this is not controversial," said David Okafor of a firearm safety coalition. "Locking devices are inexpensive and widely available. Whether or not charges are filed here, the real conversation should be about ensuring no gun is ever 'forgotten' in a closet."

Gun rights advocates caution against using individual tragedies to advance broader restrictions.

"Every responsible gun owner grieves when this happens," said a spokesperson for a firearms owners' association. "But sweeping mandates and aggressive prosecutions aren't the answer. Education and voluntary safe-storage programs have a proven track record."

## What Comes Next

The district attorney is expected to announce a decision on charges in the coming weeks. Legal observers say the outcome could hinge on how the weapon came to be stored, whether the parents knew it remained loaded, and state statutes governing negligent storage.

For now, the community is left grappling with a loss that has become painfully familiar across the country.

"Behind the legal debate is a family that will never be the same," Delgado said. "We can't lose sight of that."

*If you or someone you know needs support, resources on safe firearm storage are available through local law enforcement and national safety organizations.*
